item.dc:creator: MT newswire
item.content:encoded: 03:49 PM EDT, 08/28/2026 (MT Newswires) -- Tech stocks were lower late Friday afternoon, with the State Street Technology Select Sector SPDR ETF (XLK) falling 1.5% and the State Street SPDR S&P Semiconductor ETF (XSD) dropping 3.6%. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index was down 3.4%. In sector news, the Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security is working on a slimmed-down replacement plan for the export controls on advanced AI chips that the Biden administration imposed to slow the technological progress of geopolitical rivals, The Information reported. The new rule is expected to close a loophole via which Chinese AI firms can access advanced chips through data centers in other countries, the report said. In corporate news, Marvell Technology (MRVL) shares fell past 9% after the company's stronger-than-expected fiscal Q2 results were overshadowed by investor concerns over the timing of revenue from its deal with Alphabet's (GOOGL, GOOG) Google. Workday (WDAY) raised the low end of its full-year subscription revenue outlook after the finance and human resources solutions provider recorded fiscal Q2 results above Wall Street's estimates. Its shares climbed past 6%. Amazon.com (AMZN) has signed a power purchase agreement in Germany and invested in four Swedish wind energy projects, the company said Friday. Amazon said it agreed to buy 600 megawatts of electricity from the planned Gennaker offshore wind farm in the Baltic Sea. Amazon shares rose 3.9%. Microsoft (MSFT) workers have raised concerns about the impact of its AI data centers on energy use, water consumption, emissions, and local communities, Bloomberg reported, citing Development Chief Noelle Walsh's memo to employees. Microsoft shares were up 1.7%.

item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Det Østasiatiske Kompagni posted a net loss of DKK 0.1 million for H1 2026, narrowing from DKK 1.3 million a year earlier. Operating loss was unchanged at DKK 1.5 million, while net financial income rose to DKK 1.2 million from DKK 0.9 million. Share of profit from associates swung to DKK 0.2 million from a loss of DKK 0.6 million, reflecting Thai Poly Acrylic’s restructuring. Cash and cash equivalents slipped to DKK 7.2 million at June 30 from DKK 7.8 million at Dec. 31, with total cash flow at DKK -0.6 million. Guidance kept expected full-year operating costs at about DKK -2.3 million, with dividends seen around DKK 1.2 million and year-end cash near DKK 7 million. item.title: The most hawkish Jackson Hole speech since 2009! Walsh's debut pushes the 2-year US Treasury yield up by more than 10 basis points
item.description: The yield on the two-year U.S. Treasury note surged more than 10 basis points intraday to a one-month high. Judging by the immediate rise in the two-year Treasury yield after the speech, the market reaction to Waller's remarks even exceeded that of Powell's Jackson Hole speeches in 2022 and 2023. The swaps market is now betting that the Federal Reserve may raise rates multiple times before July next year.
item.dc:creator: 华尔街见闻
item.content:encoded: Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Walsh's debut at the Jackson Hole annual meeting was quickly priced by the bond market as a strong hawkish signal. Walsh reiterated that the Fed's 2% PCE inflation target is "firm and fixed," and stated that if there isn't confidence that underlying inflation is falling toward the target in a "clear and sufficiently rapid" manner, then the Fed "still has work to do." Market data shows that the two-year US Treasury yield rose by over 10 basis points intraday, reaching a one-month high. At the same time, market pricing for a rate hike in September has noticeably intensified. According to Bloomberg's estimates, measured by the immediate rise in the two-year Treasury yield following the speech, Walsh's remarks may be the most hawkish since 2009, with market reaction even exceeding Powell's Jackson Hole speeches in 2022 and 2023. However, Walsh did not directly commit to a rate hike in September. The core of current market trading is a more hawkish policy function: if inflation continues to exceed the target and employment and the economy remain resilient, the Fed cannot rule out the possibility of further rate hikes. Two-Year Treasury “Voting”: Walsh’s Hawkishness Surpasses Powell’s 2022 and 2023 Speeches Bloomberg’s most notable assessment this time is to compare Walsh’s speech with past market reactions to previous Jackson Hole remarks. Measured by the immediate increase in the two-year Treasury yield after the speech, Walsh’s hawkish impact may be the strongest since 2009, even surpassing Powell’s speeches in 2022 and 2023. Of course, “most hawkish since 2009” here is based on the market response of the two-year Treasury yield, rather than an absolute rating of the speech text itself. Following Bernanke's speech in 2009, the two-year yield saw an even larger full-day increase. The two-year Treasury is highly sensitive to Fed policy rates, so its rapid rise indicates traders are raising their expectations for future short-term rates. Bloomberg notes that the swap market has already begun to price in the possibility that the Fed could hike rates several times before July 2027, suggesting that this may have reassured long-term bondholders concerned about inflation. “Short End Rises, Long End Stable”: US Treasury Yield Curve Shows Hawkish Distortion Following Walsh’s speech, the US Treasury market displayed a clear trend of short-end yields rising while the long-end remained relatively stable. Market data shows the two-year Treasury yield briefly rose above 4.35%, up about 12 basis points on the day; the 10-year yield climbed about 5 basis points to 4.72%; the 30-year yield’s increase was noticeably smaller. Walsh’s comments on inflation were the direct driver of the short-end yield rise. He stated: "We must be confident that underlying inflation is moving toward our goal, and that this process is both clear and sufficiently rapid. Otherwise, we still have work to do." He also said: "I find it hard to describe overall financial conditions as restrictive." These two statements together reinforced the market’s policy judgment: inflation is not yet fully under control, and financial conditions can hardly be described as restrictive, so the Fed may still need to further dampen demand through higher policy rates. Bloomberg Intelligence rate strategist Ira Jersey believes that Walsh's insistence on the 2% inflation target, resulting in a flatter yield curve, is a reasonable market response. However, if the Fed does not tighten policy in the next one or two meetings, this trend may reverse. In other words,the market has already priced in a more hawkish Walsh, but policy actions are needed next for confirmation. Stronger US Dollar, Weaker Gold: Market Awaits “More Work to Do” to Materialize Walsh’s hawkish comments also transmitted to the foreign exchange and precious metals markets. Bloomberg points out that while swap market pricing indicates the Fed, Bank of Japan, and European Central Bank could all hike rates in September, both the US dollar against the yen and the euro moved higher after Walsh's speech. Meanwhile, gold prices weakened. Previously, markets had increased their bets on a Fed rate hike in September, and with Walsh further solidifying his anti-inflation stance, the prospect of higher rates weighed on non-yielding assets like gold. Yet Walsh still did not provide a clear policy path for the September meeting. This remains the biggest uncertainty for markets:Walsh has provided a clear anti-inflation direction, but has not committed to specific timing of actions. If the Fed does not tighten policy in the next one or two FOMC meetings, the recent surge in short-end Treasury yields, the stronger dollar, and other market reactions could partially reverse; conversely, if inflation remains stubborn and the Fed does eventually hike rates, the hawkish pricing triggered by Walsh’s Jackson Hole speech could extend further. Therefore, for the market, what this Jackson Hole debut truly leaves behind is not a definitive signal of a September rate hike, but a clearer policy condition:If inflation doesn't fall fast enough, the Fed "still has work to do."

item.title: How Does Wall Street View Waller and Jackson Hole Debut? Hawkish "Correction" of July Communication, No Rate Hike in September Could Further Harm Fed’s Credibility
item.description: The "New Fed News Agency" summarized that the Federal Reserve may not have finished its fight against inflation. The key points in Waller’s speech were that financial conditions are not restrictive and improvements in inflation are still insufficient. He did not provide a specific policy path, nor did he clearly indicate whether he supports a rate hike in September. In the U.S. Treasury market, the short end signals a need for a rate hike, while the long end remains more steady. Wall Street has not reached a consensus that a September rate increase is certain. Industry insiders believe Waller implied that the market should not expect a rate cut in the near term and should be prepared for a possible rate hike. However, while investors want GPS-level guidance, he only provided a compass, deliberately avoiding forward guidance—he spoke at length without offering substantial content.
item.dc:creator: 华尔街见闻
item.content:encoded: Federal Reserve Chair Waller’s debut at the Jackson Hole annual meeting on Friday was widely interpreted by Wall Street as a hawkish “correction” to communications following the July FOMC meeting. Waller’s speech explicitly reiterated that the Fed’s 2% inflation target is non-negotiable, argued that current overall financial conditions are not clearly restrictive, and that the recent favorable PCE and CPI results are not enough to prove substantial improvement in underlying inflation trends. He stated bluntly that unless the Fed can be “clear and fast enough” that inflation is coming down, the Fed “still has work to do.” Reuters described this as Waller’s closest admission yet that further rate hikes may be needed. Waller’s statements quickly shifted Wall Street’s focus regarding the September FOMC meeting. Priya Misra, Head of Portfolio Strategy at JPMorgan Asset Management, directly called it a “hawkish speech,” viewing Waller as firmly reiterating the Fed’s commitment to price stability, and characterized it as a “clean-up” of the “communication error” from the July press conference. Aberdeen’s Director of Investments, Matthew Amis, warned that if the Fed does not hike rates in September, its credibility may suffer again. At the same time, institutions such as Wells Fargo and Fidelis Capital believe that Waller has left sufficient room for a near-term rate hike, although some also argue that he still hasn’t clearly presented the policy path for September. Nick Timiraos, the journalist dubbed the “new Fedwire,” noted the heart of the debate: Waller believes financial conditions are not restrictive, and recent improvements in inflation data have not convinced him that underlying trends have “meaningfully improved,” yet he has not provided a specific policy path nor explicitly stated whether he supports a September rate hike. Timiraos summarized Waller’s remarks as: the Fed may not be done fighting inflation. As a result, the market is facing a more hawkish policy diagnosis, but still lacks a clear “reaction function.” CME data shows that after Waller’s speech, the probability of a rate hike in September rose from around 35% before the speech to about 50%; other market metrics briefly showed probabilities rising further to nearly 60%. Hawkish Speech Restores Anti-Inflation Credibility The most immediate impact of Waller’s speech was the “correction” at the level of policy communication. JPMorgan Asset Management’s Priya Misra was very direct in her assessment of Waller’s remarks: “This was a hawkish speech.” She believed Waller was “strongly indicating” that policymakers are committed to price stability. Misra focused on the relationship between Waller’s speech and communication following the July FOMC meeting. She called Waller’s comments a forceful response to the “communication mishap” at the July press conference: “This is a strong response to what I saw as poor communication at the July press conference.” She even described it as a “clean-up act,” a corrective closure to July’s confusion. This view was echoed by other institutional figures as well. Christopher Hodge, Chief U.S. Economist at Natixis, believes Waller’s speech was a “clear improvement” over the July press conference. Previously, the market underestimated the likelihood of further rate hikes, but now market pricing is more reasonable. Hodge said Waller strengthened his anti-inflation credibility by directly acknowledging inflation problems, reaffirming the clear 2% target, and taking responsibility for the Fed’s institutional role on inflation. Nationwide’s Chief Market Strategist Mark Hackett thought Waller accomplished his goal: communicating his stance to the market without causing major disruption. Hackett pointed out that the market had previously misjudged, believing that the 2% inflation target might be softened, but Waller made it clear that this would not happen. “He is restating his hawkish stance more consistently, not abruptly escalating it.” Hackett summarized: Do not expect a rate cut soon; be prepared for hikes. The “New Fedwire” Highlights the Core: Financial Conditions Not Restrictive, Inflation Improvement Still Lacking Timiraos’ summary of Waller’s speech was even more focused on the policy judgment itself. He noted that Waller believes overall financial conditions are not restrictive; credit and loan markets show little sign of real constraint. Meanwhile, the recent inflation data has not convinced Waller that core trends have improved. Waller’s original statement: “I find it hard to describe overall financial conditions as restrictive.” Regarding recent inflation data, Waller said: “Though PCE and CPI figures over the summer were better than expected, that is not enough for me to believe underlying trends have shown meaningful improvement.” Timiraos highlighted this sentence both in his reports and on social media. In his view, this means the market cannot rely on recent better-than-expected inflation numbers to claim Waller has shifted towards a more dovish stance. What Waller really cares about is whether the core inflation trend is sustainably and sufficiently approaching the 2% target. Waller Gives a Compass, Not a GPS Another notable feature of Waller’s speech: he clearly told the market his policy principles, yet refuses to provide a specific policy reaction function. SEI Investments Chief Investment Officer Nathan Shetty believes that since Waller directly reiterated the firmness of the 2% PCE target, his speech can only be interpreted as more hawkish. But Ellen Hazen, Chief Market Strategist at F.L. Putnam Investment Management, pointed out that Waller did not disclose the Fed’s reaction function, leaving the market still in a “black box.” Waller explained that revealing too much about the policy reaction function might constrain the Fed, much as excessive forward guidance did in 2021. Hazen believes this means Waller wants to preserve greater flexibility for the Fed in responding to economic changes, but the market may not like this approach. Peter Andersen, founder of Andersen Capital, described it vividly: Investors want a GPS, but the Fed is offering only a compass. In his view, investors want Waller to detail the economic outlook and policy path, but Waller is actually telling the market: the “new Fed” will not offer as much explicit forward guidance as past chairs; markets must adapt to this “new regime.” “If There’s No Hike in September, Credibility Takes Another Hit”: Wall Street Bets on Near-Term Action Again For markets, the most significant change is that a September hike is once again at the core of the discussion. Aberdeen’s Matthew Amis believes Waller’s speech set up a crucial scenario for the September meeting: “If they don’t hike, their credibility takes another punch.” This links Waller’s anti-inflation stance to policy action in September: since he has made clear that core inflation must fall quickly enough, or the Fed “still has work to do,” if data does not improve but there is no hike in September, the market may begin to doubt the policy weight of Waller’s preceding hawkish statements. Wells Fargo Investment Institute’s Global Strategist Gary Schlossberg also believes Waller, though not explicit, has sent signals—“connecting all the dots”—of at least one, and possibly more, rate hikes ahead. He said inflation is unlikely to fall notably—something he does not expect—and that pressure may even increase over the next 6 to 8 months. Even if there is no hike in September, he expects the Fed is likely to act later this year. Chris Gunster, Head of Fixed Income at Fidelis Capital, said outright that the market now sees the probability of a September rate hike above 50%. He argued that Waller referenced several factors—elevated inflation, a strong job market, and economic resilience—that together leave the Fed with policy space for a near-term hike. “Short End Calls for Hikes, Long End Stays Calm”: The Market Turns Waller’s Diagnosis into Trade After Waller spoke, the U.S. Treasury market reacted swiftly, especially at the short end. Reuters reported that two-year Treasury yields rose as much as 11bps to 4.34%, a one-month high; ten-year yields were up 5bps to 4.72%, with the thirty-year rising significantly less. This reveal is the market’s take on Waller’s remarks: traders are raising their pricing of near-term policy rate hikes. Michael Rosen argued that short-end Treasuries dropped and long-end yields rose, showing the market is reassessing the Fed’s policy direction—a Fed seeing inflation as the primary risk means short-term rates could climb further. Fidelis Capital’s Gunster also pointed out that short-term yields rose while long-term yields fell, making the yield curve flatter, which is consistent with markets betting on Fed hikes. However, this market reaction does not mean Wall Street has reached a consensus that a September hike is certain. Peter Cardillo, Chief Market Economist at Spartan Capital, thinks the Fed is unlikely to act in September. He believes Waller acknowledged some summer improvement in inflation, though “not yet convincing,” so the Fed may want to wait and see the inflation prints for September and October before deciding to act. In other words, the market is repricing for hikes, but data remains the ultimate gatekeeper for whether a hike will actually happen in September. Waller Still Deliberately Avoids Forward Guidance: “Said a Lot, But No Substance” Not all institutions believe Waller’s remarks have fully repaired the policy communication issues. Eugene Epstein, Head of Trading and Structured Products at Moneycorp, felt that while Waller’s speech was initially hawkish, the substance was still limited. His assessment was very pointed: “Waller said a lot, but there doesn’t seem to be much real content.” Epstein noted that Waller has sent similar hawkish signals ahead of past FOMC meetings, but policy action did not always follow. He worries the market could again be “driven by hawkish rhetoric, only to find no actual policy change” afterward. Harris Financial Group Managing Partner Jamie Cox described this style as: “Waller said a lot but actually said nothing.” He sees Waller as trying to follow a middle path, both strengthening the anti-inflation commitment and refusing to constrain future policy with forward guidance. This is precisely where the “compass not GPS” metaphor fits best: Waller is willing to tell the market what kinds of data would provoke Fed action, but not which specific meetings would see action. The Real Risk of “No Hike in September”: Not Policy, but Credibility Summing up Wall Street commentary, what matters most from Waller’s speech is not that he has promised a September hike, but that he has reestablished a more hawkish policy logic: If employment is still robust, the economy resilient, and core inflation not falling fast enough toward 2%, then current financial conditions may not be restrictive and the Fed should not rule out higher policy rates. That’s why Amis thinks if there’s no September hike, Fed credibility could take a further hit. On the other hand, Cardillo, Epstein and others remind markets: hawkish talk does not equal policy decisions. Waller still sticks to his principle of “no forward guidance,” making no clear commitment to a September hike, nor offering a mechanical policy reaction function. Thus, perhaps the more accurate Wall Street consensus is: Waller has used his Jackson Hole speech to correct July’s communication with a hawkish tone; the odds of a September hike have risen—but whether it happens ultimately depends on employment and inflation data to come. As for Waller, the real policy test is shifting from “does the market understand what he’s saying,” to a more direct question: If the data doesn’t improve significantly, is he truly willing to turn this hawkish assessment into an actual September rate hike.
